claim: In solid tumors, targeted treatments can lead to dramatic regressions, but responses are often short-lived because resistant cancer cells arise.
source: In solid tumors, targeted treatments can lead to dramatic regressions, but responses are often short-lived because resistant cancer cells arise.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract that is supported by the clinical data and modeling presented throughout the manuscript, including patient response data in Figure 1 and simulation results in Figure 2.

claim: The major strategy proposed for overcoming resistance is combination therapy.
source: The major strategy proposed for overcoming resistance is combination therapy.
evidence: This reflects established scientific consensus in oncology, as discussed in the Introduction section.

claim: 20 melanoma patients received vemurafenib treatment.
source: We first studied 20 melanoma patients receiving vemurafenib.
evidence: This is directly stated in the abstract and supported by the data presented in Figure 1 and throughout the Results section.

claim: Dual therapy results in long-term disease control for most patients if there are no single mutations that cause cross-resistance to both drugs.
source: We find that dual therapy results in long-term disease control for most patients, if there are no single mutations that cause cross-resistance to both drugs
evidence: This conclusion is derived from the mathematical model and simulations presented in the manuscript, particularly in Table 1 and Figure 3.

claim: In patients with large disease burden, triple therapy is needed.
source: in patients with large disease burden, triple therapy is needed.
evidence: This is inferred from the modeling results showing that dual therapy fails in patients with large tumor burdens when cross-resistance is possible.

claim: Simultaneous therapy with two drugs is much more effective than sequential therapy.
source: We also find that simultaneous therapy with two drugs is much more effective than sequential therapy.
evidence: This is demonstrated through modeling and simulation results presented in Figure 5.

claim: Imatinib was successful in the treatment of chronic myeloid leukemia (CML).
source: The current wave of excitement about targeted cancer therapy (Sawyers, 2004; Sequist et al., 2008; Kwak et al., 2010; Chapman et al., 2011; Gonzalez-Angulo et al., 2011) was initiated by the success of imatinib in the treatment of chronic myeloid leukemia (CML) (Druker et al., 2006; Gambacorti-Passerini et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Four decades of research passed between the discovery of the Philadelphia chromosome and the first treatment to target an activated oncogene in a human cancer.
source: Four decades of research passed between the discovery of the Philadelphia chromosome and the first treatment to target an activated oncogene in a human cancer.
evidence: This is a historical fact presented in the Introduction.

claim: Gefitinib and erlotinib are targeted therapies for non-small-cell lung cancer patients with EGFR mutations.
source: These include gefitinib and erlotinib for non-small-cell lung cancer patients with EGFR mutations (Sequist et al., 2008)
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Panitumumab and cetuximab are used for metastatic colon cancer.
source: panitumumab and cetuximab for metastatic colon cancer (Amado et al., 2008)
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Vemurafenib is used for patients with melanomas harboring BRAF mutations.
source: vemurafenib for patients with melanomas harboring BRAF mutations (Chapman et al., 2011)
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Crizotinib is used for lung cancer patients with EML4-ALK translocations.
source: crizotinib for lung cancer patients with EML4-ALK translocations (Kwak et al., 2010)
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: In most patients with solid tumors, the cancer evolves to become resistant within a few months.
source: In most patients with solid tumors, the cancer evolves to become resistant within a few months (Amado et al., 2008; Sequist et al., 2008; Gerber and Minna, 2010; Chapman et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: A small number of cells resistant to any targeted agent are always present in large solid tumors at the start of therapy.
source: One of the most important conclusions of these studies is that a small number of cells resistant to any targeted agent are always present in large solid tumors at the start of therapy and that these cells clonally expand once therapy is administered.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from previous experimental and theoretical studies cited in the text.

claim: Tumor recurrences are a fait accompli when single agents are delivered.
source: Tumor recurrences are thus a fait accompli when single agents are delivered (Diaz et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: The model is based on a multitype branching process.
source: Our model is based on a multitype branching process (see 'Materials and methods').
evidence: This is a direct statement about the methodology used in the study.

claim: Mathematical modeling has successfully predicted the dynamics of acquired resistance in colorectal cancer patients treated with panitumumab.
source: Similar mathematical modeling has successfully predicted the dynamics of acquired resistance, including the timing of treatment failure, in colorectal cancer patients treated with the EGFR inhibitor panitumumab (Diaz et al., 2012)
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Mathematical modeling has led to specific recommendations for combination therapies to treat CML.
source: and has led to specific recommendations for combination therapies to treat CML (Komarova et al., 2009; Katouli and Komarova, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: The dynamics of 68 index lesions in 20 melanoma patients receiving vemurafenib were studied.
source: To obtain key parameters for our model, we have studied the dynamics of 68 index lesions in 20 melanoma patients receiving the BRAF inhibitor vemurafenib.
evidence: This is directly stated and supported by the data presented in Figure 1.

claim: Patients P1 and P2 achieved complete responses with lesions becoming undetectable.
source: Patients P1 and P2 achieved complete responses, and their lesions became undetectable.
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and shown in Figure 1.

claim: Patient P3 had stable disease with tumors remaining approximately the same size throughout treatment.
source: Patient P3 had stable disease, with tumors remaining approximately the same size throughout treatment.
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and shown in Figure 1.

claim: Patients P4 to P6 all had partial remissions with some lesions shrinking and others unchanging or regrowing during treatment.
source: Patients P4 to P6 all had partial remissions, with some lesions shrinking and others unchanging or regrowing during treatment.
evidence: This is directly stated in the text and shown in Figure 1.

claim: The smallest lesions were the ones most likely to become undetectable when the agent was effective.
source: As expected, the smallest lesions were the ones most likely to become undetectable when the agent was effective.
evidence: This is inferred from the patient data presented in Figure 1.

claim: The average net growth rate of 21 lesions with two pretreatment measurements was calculated to be 0.01 per day.
source: For 21 lesions in our vemurafenib dataset, two pretreatment measurements were available. Using these data, we calculate the average net growth rate of these lesions to be 0.01 per day, which is consistent with previous reports (Friberg and Mattson, 1997; Eskelin et al., 2000).
evidence: This is calculated from the dataset and supported by citations to previous reports.

claim: The estimated average time between cell divisions in the absence of cell death in melanoma cells is 7 days.
source: The estimated average time between cell divisions in the absence of cell death in melanoma cells is 7 days (Rew and Wilson, 2000), implying a birth (cell division) rate of b = 0.14 per day.
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: The birth rate was set to b = 0.14 per day.
source: implying a birth (cell division) rate of b = 0.14 per day. We set this as the typical birth rate
evidence: This is a parameter choice based on literature values.

claim: The cell death rate was set to d = b − 0.01 (typical d = 0.13).
source: To achieve the observed net growth rate, we set the cell death rate to d = b − 0.01 (typical d = 0.13).
evidence: This is a parameter choice based on observed net growth rates.

claim: A cell type is defined as sensitive if the treatment would cause its death rate to exceed its birth rate.
source: A cell type is defined as sensitive if the treatment in question would cause its death rate to exceed its birth rate; otherwise, it is resistant.
evidence: This is a definition provided in the manuscript.

claim: If there is at least one possible mutation that could confer resistance to both drugs (n12 ≥ 1), then X ≈ M n12 µ.
source: If there is at least one possible mutation that could in principle confer resistance to both drugs, n12 ≥ 1, then X ≈ M n12 µ.
evidence: This is a simplification of the mathematical formula under specific conditions.

claim: The expected number of cells resistant to both drugs is independent of the numbers of mutations that confer resistance to each individual drug when n12 ≥ 1.
source: In this case, the expected number of cells resistant to both drugs is independent of the numbers of mutations, n1 and n2, that have the potential to confer resistance to each individual drug.
evidence: This is an inference from the mathematical formula.

claim: Tumor cells are much more likely to become resistant to dual therapy through one mutation conferring resistance to both drugs than through sequential mutations conferring resistance to each drug separately.
source: Intuitively, this means that tumor cells are much more likely to become resistant to dual therapy through the occurrence of one mutation conferring resistance to both drugs simultaneously than through sequential mutations conferring resistance to each drug separately.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the mathematical results.

claim: If there is no mutation that could confer resistance to both drugs simultaneously (n12 = 0), then X ≈ M n1n2 µ².
source: If there is no mutation that could confer resistance to both drugs simultaneously (no cross-resistance), then n12 = 0 and we obtain X ≈ M n1n2 µ2.
evidence: This is derived from the mathematical model under specific conditions.

claim: The expected number of cells resistant to combination therapy with k drugs, with no cross-resistance, is X ≈ M n1n2 … nk µk.
source: In general, the expected number of cells resistant to combination therapy with k drugs, with no cross-resistance, is X ≈ M n1n2 … nk µk (proof in Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is a generalization of the mathematical formula with proof in supplementary materials.

claim: The 68 lesions in the dataset declined at median rate b′ − d′ = −0.03 per day during treatment.
source: To obtain estimates for the birth rate b′ and death rate d′ of sensitive cells during treatment, we calculate that the 68 lesions in our dataset declined at median rate b′ − d′ = −0.03 per day (−0.01 and −0.07 being 10th and 90th percentile, respectively).
evidence: This is calculated from the patient dataset.

claim: The typical death rate of sensitive cells during treatment was set to d′ = b′ + 0.03.
source: Thus, we set the typical death rate of sensitive cells during treatment to d′ = b′ + 0.03
evidence: This is a parameter choice based on observed decline rates.

claim: About 50 different mutations can confer resistance to a typical targeted therapeutic agent.
source: Previous studies (Engelman et al., 2007; Corcoran et al., 2010; Diaz et al., 2012; Ellis et al., 2012; Misale et al., 2012; Straussman et al., 2012; Wilson et al., 2012) suggest that about 50 different mutations can confer resistance to a typical targeted therapeutic agent.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: Monotherapy will eventually fail in all lesions that can be detected by conventional imaging when there are 50 or more potential resistance mutations.
source: Assuming that there are 50 or more potential resistance mutations, monotherapy will eventually fail in all lesions that can be detected by conventional imaging (Figure 2A,B)
evidence: This is demonstrated through computer simulations shown in Figure 2A and 2B.

claim: Small lesions can decrease below the detection limit and appear to be eradicated for years before re-emerging.
source: Small lesions, however, can decrease below the detection limit and appear to be eradicated for years before re-emerging (Figure 2B,C).
evidence: This is demonstrated through computer simulations shown in Figure 2B and 2C.

claim: Tumors can recur after long periods of remission without the need to invoke processes involving cancer stem cells, angiogenesis, or immune escape.
source: This result is important, as it explains why tumors can recur after long periods of remission without the need to invoke processes involving cancer stem cells, angiogenesis, or immune escape (Hensel et al., 2012).
evidence: This is an inference from the simulation results and supported by citation.

claim: 22 patients with metastatic disease were studied: 7 with pancreatic ductal adenocarcinomas, 11 with colorectal carcinomas, and 6 with melanomas.
source: To determine the total extent of disease in typical patients who enroll for clinical trials, we quantified all radiographically detectable metastases in 22 such patients: 7 with pancreatic ductal adenocarcinomas, 11 with colorectal carcinomas, and 6 with melanomas
evidence: This is directly stated and data are presented in Table 1.

claim: The number of metastatic lesions in the 22 patients ranged from 1 to 30.
source: The number of metastatic lesions in the 22 patients described in Table 1 ranged from 1 to 30
evidence: This is directly stated and data are presented in Table 1.

claim: The total tumor burden in the 22 patients ranged from 9 × 10⁸ to 3 × 10¹¹ cells.
source: and their total tumor burden ranged from 9 × 108 to 3 × 1011 cells (see Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is directly stated and data are presented in Table 1 and Supplementary file 2.

claim: Monotherapy will fail in all 22 patients studied.
source: We find that monotherapy will fail in all 22 patients (Table 1 and Supplementary file 3), as expected from the simulations in Figure 2A–C and from clinical experience.
evidence: This is calculated using the model and presented in Table 1.

claim: If there is even one possible mutation that can confer resistance to both drugs, dual therapy has only a small chance of curing patients.
source: If there is even one possible mutation that can in principle confer resistance to both drugs, then our model shows that dual therapy has also only a small chance of curing patients, even those with the smallest tumor burden.
evidence: This is calculated using the model and presented in Table 1.

claim: None of the 22 patients are expected to be cured by dual therapy if there is one cross-resistance mutation.
source: In our cohort of 22 patients, none are expected to be cured under these circumstances (Table 1).
evidence: This is calculated using the model and presented in Table 1.

claim: Eight patients with the smallest tumor burden would have >95% probability of cure with dual therapy if there are no cross-resistance mutations.
source: In the cohort described in Table 1, we calculate that eight patients (those with the smallest tumor burden) would have >95% probability of cure.
evidence: This is calculated using the model and presented in Table 1.

claim: Patients with the largest tumor burden would have a >20% probability of tumor recurrence even with dual therapy without cross-resistance.
source: Those with the largest tumor burden would still have a >20% probability of tumor recurrence.
evidence: This is calculated using the model and presented in Table 1.

claim: Therapy with three agents will not cure patients if there is even one mutation that can confer resistance to all three agents.
source: Additional simulations show that therapy with three agents will also not cure patients if there is even one mutation that can confer resistance to all three agents.
evidence: This is demonstrated through additional simulations.

claim: In patients with high cell turnover (time between cell divisions of 1 day), dual therapy with no cross-resistance would fail in 37% of patients described in Table 1.
source: We note that in patients whose tumors have high cell turnover (time between cell divisions of 1 day, corresponding to b = 1), even dual therapy with no cross-resistance mutations would be expected to fail in 37% of patients described in Table 1 (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is calculated using the model with different parameter values.

claim: If there is one genetic alteration that can confer resistance to two targeted agents, therapy with those agents will not result in sustained benefit for the majority of patients with advanced disease.
source: Most importantly, they show that even if there is one genetic alteration within any of the 6.6 billion base pairs present in a human diploid cell that can confer resistance to two targeted agents, therapy with those agents will not result in sustained benefit for the majority of patients with advanced disease.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the modeling results presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: The same result is obtained with triple therapy if there is the possibility of a mutation conferring cross-resistance to three drugs.
source: The same result is obtained with triple therapy; if there is the possibility of a mutation conferring cross-resistance to three drugs, lesions of the size commonly observed in patients with advanced cancers will always recur.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the modeling results.

claim: A combination of three current targeted drugs for CML will not be beneficial over a combination of two such drugs due to cross-resistance.
source: Similar conclusions were reached by Komarova et al. (2009), who showed that a combination of three current targeted drugs for CML will not be beneficial over a combination of two such drugs due to cross-resistance.
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Increased expression of growth factors such as hepatocyte growth factor can confer resistance to a variety of drugs that inhibit kinases functioning through different pathways.
source: For example, it has been shown that the increased expression of growth factors (such as hepatocyte growth factor) can confer resistance to a variety of drugs that inhibit kinases functioning through different pathways (Straussman et al., 2012; Wilson et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Mutations in several different genes, including those encoding ABC transporters, can confer resistance to many different drugs.
source: Moreover, it is well known that mutations in several different genes, including those encoding ABC transporters, can confer resistance to many different drugs (Lavi et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Sequential administration of targeted agents precludes any chance for cure even when there are no possible mutations that can confer cross-resistance.
source: Our data show that this sequential administration precludes any chance for cure—even when there are no possible mutations that can confer cross-resistance (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is demonstrated through modeling results shown in Figure 5C.

claim: When there are potential mutations conferring cross-resistance to two or more agents, simultaneous administration offers some hope for cure while there is no hope with sequential therapy.
source: And when there are potential mutations conferring cross-resistance to two or more agents, simultaneous administration offers some hope for cure while there is no hope with sequential therapy (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is demonstrated through modeling results shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Tumor growth and evolution is modeled as a continuous time multitype branching process.
source: We model tumor growth and evolution as a continuous time multitype branching process (Athreya and Ney, 1972; Goldie and Coldman, 1998; Komarova and Wodarz, 2005).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the methodology with supporting citations.

claim: In the case of two drugs, there are four possible cell types: 00, 01, 10, and 11.
source: In the case of two drugs, there are four possible types: 00, 01, 10, and 11, where zeros indicate sensitivity to a drug and ones indicate resistance.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the model structure.

claim: The pretreatment phase is initiated with a single fully sensitive cell (type 00 for two drugs).
source: The pretreatment phase is initiated with a single fully sensitive cell (type 00 for two drugs).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the model assumptions.

claim: During the pretreatment phase, all cell types reproduce at rate b and die at rate d.
source: During this phase, all cell types reproduce at rate b and die at rate d.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the model parameters.

claim: The pretreatment phase ends when there are a total of M cells.
source: The pretreatment phase ends, and the treatment phase begins, when there are a total of M cells.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the model structure.

claim: During the treatment phase, all cell types that are sensitive to one or more drugs have birth rate b' and death rate d'.
source: During the treatment phase, all cell types that are sensitive to one or more drugs have birth rate b' and death rate d'
evidence: This is a direct statement about the model parameters during treatment.

claim: Fully resistant cells maintain the pretreatment birth and death rates during treatment.
source: fully resistant cells maintain the pretreatment birth and death rates.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the model assumptions.

claim: The mathematical analysis of dual therapy is based on an exact solution to the two-type branching process.
source: Our mathematical analysis of dual therapy is based in part on a recently discovered exact solution to the two-type branching process (Antal and Krapivsky, 2011).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the methodology with supporting citation.

claim: Monte Carlo computer simulations were used to confirm analytical results.
source: We use Monte Carlo computer simulations to confirm our analytical results and improve our understanding of the evolutionary dynamics during cancer treatment.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the methodology.

claim: For cell subpopulations with less than 10⁴ cells, the process is simulated exactly.
source: For cell subpopulations with less than 104 cells, the process is simulated exactly
evidence: This is a direct statement about the simulation methodology.

claim: For larger subpopulations, a deterministic (exponential growth) approximation is used.
source: for larger subpopulations, a deterministic (exponential growth) approximation is used in the interest of efficiency.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the simulation methodology.

claim: Between 10⁶ and 10⁸ runs are used for each parameter combination in simulations.
source: Between 106 and 108 runs are used for each parameter combination.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the simulation methodology.

claim: With sequential therapy, if there is even a single mutation that confers cross-resistance to both drugs (n12 = 1), then sequential therapy will fail in all cases.
source: When there is a possibility of a single mutation conferring resistance to both drugs, sequential combination therapy will 'always' fail.
evidence: This is demonstrated through modeling results shown in Figure 5A.

claim: In approximately 74% of lesions with cross-resistance, failure is due to mutations present prior to treatment with the first drug.
source: In ∼74% of lesions, the failure is due to mutations that were present prior to the treatment with the first drug
evidence: This is calculated from simulation results shown in Figure 5A.

claim: In approximately 26% of lesions with cross-resistance, failure is due to development of cells resistant to drug 2 during treatment with drug 1.
source: whereas in ∼26% of the lesions, failure is due to the development of cells resistant to drug 2 during treatment with drug 1 (Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is calculated from simulation results shown in Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: With simultaneous treatment when cross-resistance mutations are possible, it is possible to eradicate approximately 26% of lesions.
source: With simultaneous treatment, it is possible to eradicate ∼26% of the lesions even when cross-resistance mutations are possible (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is demonstrated through modeling results shown in Figure 5B.

claim: When there is no possibility of a mutation conferring cross-resistance to both drugs, sequential therapy fails in 100% of cases.
source: When there is no possibility of a mutation conferring cross-resistance to both drugs, the differences are even more striking: sequential therapy fails in 100% of cases (Figure 5C)
evidence: This is demonstrated through modeling results shown in Figure 5C.

claim: When there is no cross-resistance, simultaneous therapy succeeds in >99% of lesions of identical size.
source: whereas simultaneous therapy succeeds in >99% of lesions of the identical size (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is demonstrated through modeling results shown in Figure 5D.

claim: If cancer stem cells represent only 0.1% of cancer cells, then the development of resistance to single agents or combinations is roughly 0.1% as likely as if 100% of cancer cells have the capacity to repopulate the tumor.
source: For example, if cancer stem cells represent only 0.1% of cancer cells, then the development of resistance to single agents or combinations is roughly 0.1% as likely as if 100% of the cancer cells have the capacity to repopulate the tumor.
evidence: This is an inference from the model when considering cancer stem cell dynamics.

claim: The fraction of cancer stem cells in CML appears to be low, perhaps explaining the remarkable success of imatinib.
source: The fraction of cancer stem cells appears to be this low in CML, perhaps explaining the remarkable success of imatinib (Michor et al., 2005).
evidence: This is an inference supported by citation to published literature.

claim: In solid tumors, the fraction of cancer stem cells seems much higher, usually higher than 5% and in some cases close to 100%.
source: In solid tumors, however, the fraction of cancer stem cells seems much higher, usually higher than 5% and in some cases close to 100% (Shackleton et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: Non-stem cells can convert to cancer stem cells under certain conditions.
source: This issue is further complicated by the fact that the situation is plastic, with non-stem cells converting to cancer stem cells under certain conditions (Gupta et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published literature.

claim: If resistance has a fitness cost, then we expect a smaller number of resistant cells at the start of treatment and correspondingly a higher chance of treatment success.
source: If resistance has a fitness cost, then we expect a smaller number of resistant cells at the start of treatment and correspondingly a higher chance of treatment success.
evidence: This is an inference from the model that is tested through simulations.

claim: For combination therapies with drugs that have resistance mutations in common, the probability of eradicating a lesion is only marginally affected by costly resistance.
source: For combination therapies with drugs that have resistance mutations in common, the probability of eradicating a lesion is only marginally affected by costly resistance.
evidence: This is demonstrated through simulation results shown in Table 2.

claim: For dual therapies with no cross-resistance mutations, treatment has a high chance of eradicating all but the largest lesions, whether or not resistance is costly.
source: For dual therapies with no cross-resistance mutations, treatment has a high chance of eradicating all but the largest lesions, whether or not resistance is costly.
evidence: This is demonstrated through simulation results shown in Table 2.

claim: If each resistance mutation decreases the net growth rate of cells by 10%, the probability that dual therapy with no cross-resistance mutations will eradicate a lesion of size 10¹¹ in which cells divide on average every day is 68%.
source: For example, if each resistance mutation decreases the net growth rate of cells by 10%, the probability that dual therapy with no cross-resistance mutations will eradicate a lesion of size 1011 in which cells divide on average every day is 68% (compared with 47% in the case of neutral resistance).
evidence: This is calculated from simulation results.

claim: The rate b′ − d′ of tumor decline is of primary importance, and whether this is achieved by eliminating cells or suppressing division has only a minor effect on treatment outcomes.
source: Overall, the rate b′ − d′ of tumor decline is of primary importance, and whether this is achieved by eliminating cells or suppressing division has only a minor effect on treatment outcomes.
evidence: This is an inference from the model analysis.

claim: If dual therapy shrinks a tumor at rate −0.03 per day by increasing cell death, the eradication probability is 26%.
source: For example, consider a dual therapy with n1 = n2 = 50, n12 = 1, applied to a lesion of size M = 109, with other parameters as inferred from our dataset. If this therapy shrinks the tumor at rate −0.03 per day by increasing cell death, the eradication probability is 26%.
evidence: This is calculated from the model.

claim: If the therapy suppresses division instead of increasing cell death, the eradication probability increases to 29%.
source: If the therapy instead suppresses division, this probability increases to 29%, because there are fewer chances for resistance mutations during treatment.
evidence: This is calculated from the model.

claim: The parameters with the strongest effects on the success of combination treatments are lesion sizes and point mutation rate.
source: The parameters with the strongest effects on the success of combination treatments—apart from the number of cross-resistance mutations—are lesion sizes and point mutation rate.
evidence: This is an inference from the model analysis.

claim: Combination treatments will be more effective in cancers with small fractions of tumor stem cells.
source: Thus, we expect that combination treatments will be more effective in cancers with small fractions of tumor stem cells (small effective population size of lesions)
evidence: This is an inference from the model analysis.

claim: Combination treatments will be less effective in cancers with significantly increased point mutation rates.
source: and less effective in cancers with significantly increased point mutation rates.
evidence: This is an inference from the model analysis.

claim: The results are not readily applicable to therapies that rely on the immune destruction of tumors.
source: Our results are not readily applicable to therapies that rely on the immune destruction of tumors (Kirkwood et al., 2012), such as those employing CTLA-4 (Hodi et al., 2010), PD1 (Topalian et al., 2012), or CD19-CARs (Grupp et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the limitations of the model with supporting citations.

claim: Long-term control of disease is more common with immune modulators than with small molecule drugs.
source: Once the mechanisms underlying the failures of immune modulators become more apparent, it will be important to try to understand why long-term control of disease is more common with these therapies than with small molecule drugs.
evidence: This is stated as an observation with supporting citations.

claim: The minimal detection size was assumed to be approximately 63 × 10⁶ cells.
source: The minimal detection size (indicated by discontinuous red line) was assumed to be ≈63 × 106 cells.
evidence: This is stated in the Figure 1 caption.

claim: Results similar to those obtained by simulation are observed in several of the individual lesions from actual patients graphed in Figure 1.
source: Note that results similar to those obtained by simulation are observed in several of the individual lesions from actual patients graphed in Figure 1.
evidence: This is a comparison between simulation results and actual patient data.
